summary:
Moquegua department stands under Peru's national framework. Consensual same-sex activity has not been criminalised since the 1924 Penal Code, trans identity is not an offence, and the age of consent is 14 regardless of gender or sexual orientation under a 2012 Constitutional Court decision. No Moquegua-specific trans statute, municipal ordinance, court finding or enforcement action appears in the sources; the national rules described below bind the department directly.

Two legislative stages restrict which public restrooms a trans visitor may use. On 20 February 2025 the Congress' Commission on Women and Family approved without dissent a dictamen covering bills 6506 and 8457, barring entry to public sanitary facilities designated for a sex other than one's birth sex, with exceptions limited to custody, medical care, or accompanying an adult, a child under 12 or a disabled person, and requiring unambiguous signage; at publication the measure still awaited plenary backing. Trans-rights activist Gianna Camacho called it discriminatory and warned that security staff would apply their own criteria, for example by demanding a DNI at the door.

On 2 April 2025 the Congress plenary approved, exempt from a second vote, the law strengthening the right to sexual integrity of children and adolescents. Its Article 5 bars anyone whose biological sex does not match the facility's intended sex from public sanitary facilities, with exceptions only for accompanying or assisting minors, patients or people with specific needs. An analysis by Miriam Tovar and Gonzalo Ugarte of the IDEHPUCP institute at the Pontifical Catholic University of Peru (15 April 2025) states that the measure implicitly brands trans people as more likely to enter bathrooms to harass or sexually abuse minors, conditions basic rights on verifiable 'biological sex', and violates equality, non-discrimination and gender self-determination; the same institute's published position invokes Inter-American Court of Human Rights Advisory Opinion OC-24/17, under which gender identity falls within protected personal autonomy. The authors note that Congress had already banned inclusive language and again rejected equal marriage.

Recorded violence against trans people is rising and the figures understate it. The TLGBI Rights Observatory's annual report, covered by Agencia Presentes on 22 July 2024, records 54 killings of TLGBI people and 170 rights-violation cases in Peru between 2020 and 2023, with trans women the most affected. The report recounts the February 2023 kidnapping of trans woman Rubí Torres Silvano, 31, in central Lima and her murder in Carabayllo with approximately 30 shots at the hands of the 'Los Gallegos' gang; the bodies showed gunshot wounds, stab wounds and throat-slitting indicating extreme hate. These national figures describe the risk environment a trans visitor to Moquegua enters, and no departmental breakdown is available.

Peru also has documented protection machinery of first-instance significance. The torture and rape of trans activist Azul Rojas Marín ended on 15 December 2025 with 17 years' imprisonment for police officers Dino Ponce, Luis Quispe and Juan León, the country's first conviction in a case motivated by sexual discrimination and, per BBC News Mundo, the Inter-American Court of Human Rights' first torture-by-discrimination case in the region.
tangentialFactors:
Peru is one of only three South American countries, with Paraguay and Guyana, without LGBT anti-discrimination coverage in law. Government Decree Nº 1323 had criminalised discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation and gender identity from 7 January 2017 through Articles 46 and 323 of the Penal Code; Congress voted 66–29 in May 2017 to strip the provisions, President Kuczynski's veto stood at that point, and the protections were removed as the Penal Code was reworked, the repeal carried by Popular Force and Alliance for Progress members after an April Constitutional Committee vote and a petition carrying one million signatures.

Human Rights Watch reports that the April 2025 sexual-integrity law also mandates that public-restroom entry be determined by 'biological sex', applies to trans youth, and contains vaguely worded child-protection provisions, notably Article 4 on media and advertising and Article 5, that enable censorship of identity-related, artistic and educational content, while the minimum sentence for obscenity rose from three to four years. Human Rights Watch characterises child protection as a pretext for repression and the scapegoating of trans people.

Institutional hostility is documented alongside the legislative measures. Outright International reports that public institutions themselves contribute to anti-LGBTIQ discrimination; in July 2025 a Lima constitutional court, after an activist legal challenge, struck an anti-equality decree as unconstitutional; and an April 2025 law on foreign funding of NGOs lets authorities revoke registrations on 'public order and security' grounds, a power that risks being used against queer organising. In April 2025 television presenter Ana María Salcedo of Willax TV publicly harassed the first openly-lesbian congresswoman, Susel Paredes, telling her to 'go use the men's room'.

A 2012 Universidad Peruana Cayetano Heredia study found that 70% of trans women in Lima and Callao work in sex work, a documented exposure factor for police and public violence; the figure is a capital-region estimate and is not a Moquegua measurement. Co-author Gianna Camacho, a trans human-rights defender and journalist, states that recorded hate-crime numbers are only a sub-registry.
localsOnly:
Legal recognition of gender is partially available to Peruvian residents. Transgender Peruvians may change their legal name to match their gender identity. In 2014 the Constitutional Court barred gender-marker changes on national identity documents, then reversed itself in a ruling of 21 October 2016 published 8 November, permitting gender change through a judicial process without sex-reassignment surgery. A Gender Identity Law covering legal gender change without surgery and access to passports and other identity documents matching gender identity was introduced on 4 November 2016 and remained pending in the legislature as of March 2021.

Healthcare classification has shifted in both directions. In May 2024 the government decreed 'transsexualism' a mental health problem in order to cover trans healthcare; after protests, MINSA revised the term to 'gender discordance' in June 2024 for health-insurance classification purposes, and in June 2024 health authorities removed outdated pathologising terminology for gender diversity from official health guidance, described by Human Rights Watch as a step toward dignity for trans patients. Conversion therapy is banned for medical professionals, and in May 2024 MINSA reiterated that sexual orientation and gender identity are not diseases, a protection with direct bearing on trans and LGBTQ minors exposed to such practices.

Residents live under the same national statutes described for visitors, including the sexual-integrity law's restroom provision and the absence of Penal Code hate-crime coverage, and they additionally face the identity-document and health-insurance procedures above.
